title: How to Photograph Reflective and Metallic Products Without a Studio Nightmare
description: Metal, chrome, mirror finish products are hard to shoot. Here's the workflow that solves reflection problems for good.

blocks.text: Metallic and reflective products—watches, chrome hardware, mirror-finish accessories, polished jewelry—are the hardest professional photography discipline. Everything they touch shows up in the reflection. Your face. Your camera. Your ceiling.
Here's how to fix it without hiring a specialist.
Why Reflective Products Are Hard
Reflections capture:
The result: a photo where the "product" is actually a photo of your room in the product. Not what buyers want.
The Diffusion Technique
Step 1: Wrap your product in a "light tent"—a translucent enclosure that diffuses light from all angles.
DIY version: A cardboard box with sides cut out and covered with white parchment paper. Total cost: $2.
Step 2: Shoot through a small hole in the front.
Reflections now show only the diffused white surroundings. Product looks like it's in a professional studio.
The Editing Cleanup
Even with diffusion, some reflections remain. Handle them at edit-photo.com:

items.text: Keep reflections that describe the material (subtle highlights)

blocks.text: The Background Question
Reflective products photograph best on:
Never colored backgrounds—the color bleeds into the product's reflection and looks fake.
At edit-photo.com, test both black and white versions. Choose based on platform.
For Watches Specifically
Watches are the ultimate reflective challenge. Chrome case, glass crystal, metal bracelet—everything reflects.
Standard watch photography:

items.text: Detail: crown, hands, dial texture, caseback markings

blocks.text: For Jewelry (Fine Metals)

items.text: Slight overhead angle to catch the light on facets
Dark background for gold/silver contrast (shows depth)
Then swap to white for marketplace via edit-photo.com

blocks.text: The Reflection You Want
Not all reflections are bad. Subtle highlights on a metal surface make the product look expensive. Total flat matte finish looks cheap.
Rule: Keep 20-30% of the natural reflection (aesthetic). Remove 70-80% (environmental).

The current edit-photo tool isolates a foreground subject; it is not a general object-removal or inpainting tool. For unwanted people or objects inside the scene, reshoot, crop, or use a licensed editor designed for that task.
